questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/d15f201b8f2a8521c68321b9ce15e5b13091fc899728822526d11cdcee08a393.png)

The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=2-\frac{6}{x+1}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=5$ is given by the following integral expression below: 

$$
A=-\,{\int }_{1}^{a}(2-\frac{6}{x+1})\text{d}x+{\int }_{a}^{5}(2-\frac{6}{x+1})\text{d}x
$$

Find the value of $a.$ Do not round the answer.

$a=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=2-\frac{6}{x+1}.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{6}{x+1} & =0 \\ -\frac{6}{x+1} & =-2 \\ \frac{6}{x+1} & =2 \\ 6 & =2(x+1) \\ 6 & =2x+2 \\ 4 & =2x \\ 2 & =x \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=1$ and $x=5$ is $x=2.$

Since $2\in [1,5],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=2$ to $x=5.$

So, $a=2$ and the final expression will be

$$
A=\,-\,{\int }_{1}^{2}(2-\frac{6}{x+1})\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{5}(2-\frac{6}{x+1})\text{d}x.
$$

The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y={x}^{2}+3x$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-4$ to $x=-1$ is given by the integral expression below. What is the value of $a?$

$$
A={\int }_{-4}^{a}({x}^{2}+3x)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{a}^{-1}({x}^{2}+3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y={x}^{2}+3x.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{2}+3x \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+3x \\ x(x+3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=0$ or $x=-3.$ The only solution between $x=-4$ and $x=-1$ is $x=-3.$

Since $-3\in [-4,-1]$, we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-4$ to $x=-3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=-1.$

So, $a=-3$ and the final expression will be

$$
A={\int }_{-4}^{-3}({x}^{2}+3x)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-3}^{-1}({x}^{2}+3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is given by the integral expression below. What is the value of $a?$

$$
A={\int }_{-1}^{a}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x-{\int }_{a}^{5/2}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4} & =0 \\ -\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4} & =-4 \\ {x}^{4} & =16 \\ \sqrt[4]{{x}^{4}} & =\pm \sqrt[4]{16} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt[4]{{2}^{4}} \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution between $x=-1$ and $x=\frac{5}{2}$ is $x=2.$

Since $2\in [-1,\frac{5}{2}],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=2.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=2$ to $x=\frac{5}{2}.$

So, $a=2$ and the final expression will be

$$
A={\int }_{-1}^{2}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{5/2}(4-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})\text{d}x.
$$

The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=\frac{4}{x-2}+1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-5$ to $x=0$ is given by the integral expression below. What is the value of $a?$

$$
A={\int }_{-5}^{a}(\frac{4}{x-2}+1)\text{d}x-{\int }_{a}^{0}(\frac{4}{x-2}+1)\text{d}x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=\frac{4}{x-2}+1.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{x-2}+1 & =0 \\ \frac{4}{x-2} & =-1 \\ 4 & =-(x-2) \\ 4 & =-x+2 \\ 2 & =-x \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-2\in [-5,0],$ we have two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-5$ to $x=-2.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$

So, $a=-2$ and the final expression will be

$$
A={\int }_{-5}^{-2}(\frac{4}{x-2}+1)\text{d}x-{\int }_{-2}^{0}(\frac{4}{x-2}+1)\text{d}x.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Area Bounded Between the X-Axis and a Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/cd6555800f4b7c7a7ae76ef9dd75ebca543ea4898b4205dd24df15f52f95653d.png)

Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=-4{x}^{3}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=1,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0\in [-1,1]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

For $x\in [-1,0]$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}-4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{x}^{4}\,{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the region for $x\in [0,1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis.  Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}-4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}-4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-0) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=1+1=2.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/14bd6415062b5e08f183e22059cffa2893442c87c391dfdb1c020c942e15af83.png)

Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=1,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0\in [-1,1]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Notice that the region for $x\in [-1,0]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [0,1],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{8}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+6x-5 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-6x+5 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-5) & =0 \\ x & =1,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

Since $5\in [2,7],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=2$ to $x=5.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=5$ to $x=7.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/e14a891e924a6911a0df962dc5c5b41c90b0c411de4ebe1f7e52ec1953e4124c.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [5,7]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{5}^{7}(-{x}^{2}+6x-5)\text{d}x
$$

will be negative.

Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{2}^{5}(-{x}^{2}+6x-5)\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{2}^{5}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+6{\int }_{2}^{5}x\,\text{d}x-5{\int }_{2}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{2}^{5}+3{x}^{2}\,{|}_{2}^{5}-5x\,{|}_{2}^{5} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{5}^{3}-{2}^{3}]+3[{5}^{2}-{2}^{2}]-5[5-2] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(125-8)+3(25-4)-5(3) \\  & =-\frac{117}{3}+63-15 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [5,7],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{5}^{7}(-{x}^{2}+6x-5)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{7}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-6{\int }_{5}^{7}x\,\text{d}x+5{\int }_{5}^{7}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{5}^{7}-3{x}^{2}\,{|}_{5}^{7}+5x\,{|}_{5}^{7} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[{7}^{3}-{5}^{3}]-3[{7}^{2}-{5}^{2}]+5[7-5] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(343-125)-3(49-25)+5(2) \\  & =\frac{218}{3}-72+10 \\  & =\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =9+\frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{59}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=3x-{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(3-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $3\in [1,4],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/219d7aa5b976c97d47a96d0c94c3d61d139d5ddddc55b82d0df68f19ad6d5149.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [3,4]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{3}^{4}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{3}x\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[{3}^{2}-{1}^{2}]-\frac{1}{3}[{3}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[9-1]-\frac{1}{3}[27-1] \\  & =12-\frac{26}{3} \\  & =\frac{10}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [3,4],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{3}^{4}(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3{\int }_{3}^{4}x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{3}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[{4}^{2}-{3}^{2}]+\frac{1}{3}[{4}^{3}-{3}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}[16-9]+\frac{1}{3}[64-27] \\  & =-\frac{21}{2}+\frac{37}{3} \\  & =\frac{11}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{10}{3}+\frac{11}{6}=\frac{31}{6}.
$$

Find the total area of the region between the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2\in [0,3],$ we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=2$ to $x=3.$

Notice that the region for $x\in [0,2]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{2}+{x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{2}^{3}-{0}^{3}]+[{2}^{2}-{0}^{2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[8-0]+4 \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}+4 \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [2,3],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{2}^{3}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-2{\int }_{2}^{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}\,{|}_{2}^{3}-{x}^{2}\,{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[{3}^{3}-{2}^{3}]-[{3}^{2}-{2}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[27-8]-[9-4] \\  & =\frac{19}{3}-5 \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{4}{3}+\frac{4}{3}=\frac{8}{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=9-{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=6.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}9-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-3)(x+3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-3$ and $x=3$ are our real solutions. Since $3\in [-3,6]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=6.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/70df9534ea4f69993871888a5f751ecd6aea9d1e0aaaf128d55442d9913b3dd5.png)

For $x\in [-3,3]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}(9-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =9{\int }_{-3}^{3}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =9x{|}_{-3}^{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =[9(3)-9(-3)]-[\frac{(3)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =54-18 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x\in [3,6]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-3}^{6}(9-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{-3}^{6}(9-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-9{\int }_{3}^{6}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{6}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-9x{|}_{3}^{6}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{3}^{6} \\  & =-9[6-3]+[\frac{(6)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(3)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =-27+63 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=36+36=72.
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=27-3{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=5.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}27-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =27 \\ {x}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-3$ and $x=3$ are our real solutions. Since $3\in [-3,5]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=3.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=3$ to $x=5.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/6b3ca7be487585b296aaeb0b3fa7eb4ce8b9b4f9ad35d52baefa04f2fbbed621.png)

For $x\in [-3,3]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =27{\int }_{-3}^{3}\,\text{d}x-3{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =27x{|}_{-3}^{3}-{x}^{3}{|}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =27[3-(-3)]-[(3)^{3}-(-3)^{3}] \\  & =162-54 \\  & =108.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x\in [3,5]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{3}^{5}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{3}^{5}(27-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-27{\int }_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{3}^{5}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-27x{|}_{3}^{5}+{x}^{3}{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =-27[5-3]+[(5)^{3}-(3)^{3}] \\  & =-54+98 \\  & =44.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=108+44=152.
$$

questions.problem:

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y={x}^{5}-x$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{4}-1) & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1)({x}^{2}+1) & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x(x-1)(x+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=\pm 1$ or $x=0.$ 
This gives us two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

For $x\in [-1,0]$, we have

$$
{A}_{1}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that for $x\in [0,1]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{2}=-{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}-({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}-({x}^{5}-x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The total area $A$ of the region between the curve $y=x^3-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=2$ is given by the integral expression below. What is the value of $a?$

$$
A = \displaystyle -\int_{-2}^{a} (x^3-1) \:\textrm{d}x + \int_{a}^{2} (x^3-1) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/57d01ea60e3cd9770f2ef978e46e2cef7b69a9fcdc2ac478d5b6c73d8f366c7b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To determine the missing limit of integration, we need to find the $x$-intercept of the curve $y=x^3-1.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{3}-1 \\ (0) & ={x}^{3}-1 \\ {x}^{3} & =1 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1 \in [-2,2]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x={\color{blue}{1}}.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x={\color{blue}{1}}$ to $x=2.$

So, $a={\color{blue}1}$ and the final expression will be

$$
A = \displaystyle -\int_{-2}^{\color{blue}1} (x^3-1) \:\textrm{d}x + \int_{\color{blue}1}^{2} (x^3-1) \:\textrm{d}x.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x^3$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=\dfrac{3}{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/0d3ede3cfbec765228ea184c74e0cb35f1df2a9340bd1cb703a0990249fecf30.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0 \in \left[-1,\dfrac{3}{2}\right]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{3}{2}.$

Notice that for $x \in  [-1,0]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
\int_{a}^{b} y(x) \:\textrm{d}x = \int_{-1}^{0}  \dfrac{x^3}{2}  \:\textrm{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
A_1 = -\int_{-1}^{0}  \dfrac{x^3}{2}  \:\textrm{d}x .
$$

For $x \in\left[0,\dfrac{3}{2}\right]$, we have

$$
A_2 = \int_{0}^{3/2}\dfrac{x^3}{2} \:\textrm{d}x.
$$

The total area is

$$
A = A_1+A_2 = - \int_{-1}^{0} \dfrac{x^3}{2}  \:\textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{3/2} \dfrac{x^3}{2}  \:\textrm{d}x .
$$

 

Finally, we carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =-{\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}]}_{-1}^{0}+{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}]}_{0}^{3/2} \\  & =-[0-\frac{1}{8}]+[\frac{81}{128}-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}+\frac{81}{128} \\  & =\frac{97}{128}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y=x^3-9x$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-9x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-9) & =0 \\ x(x-3)(x+3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0,$ $x=-3,$ and $x=3$ are our real solutions. Since $0 \in [-3,3]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-3$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013598/assets/29a51c9892de59037e84bace2f8b5822222c3056a05af861cbd741390a437a61.png)

For $x \in [-3,0]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}({x}^{3}-9x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-9{\int }_{-3}^{0}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}{|}_{-3}^{0}-\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-3}^{0} \\  & =[0-\frac{(-3)^{4}}{4}]-9[0-\frac{(-3)^{2}}{2}] \\  & =-\frac{81}{4}+\frac{81}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for $x \in [0,3]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
\int_{a}^{b} y(x) \:\textrm{d}x = \int_{0}^{3} \left(x^3-9x\right) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{3}-9x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+9{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}{|}_{0}^{3}+\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-[\frac{(3)^{4}}{4}-0]+9[\frac{(3)^{2}}{2}-0] \\  & =-\frac{81}{4}+\frac{81}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A = A_1+A_2 =  \dfrac{81}{4} + \dfrac{81}{4} = \dfrac{81}{2}.
$$
